## 1. Goal

Make every report figure look consistent and readable in print, including greyscale: one style function, a fixed look per scheduler, and a helper that saves each figure as PNG and PDF. Every later figure uses it.

## 2. Background

**From PRD §11.3b Figures prompt:**

```
You are helping Ahaana build tools/plot_figures.py for the Adaptive Priority Resource Manager. Ahaana is learning.
Context: docs/PRD.md section 5 "Summary CSV formats"; docs/BLUEPRINT.md section 6 (experiments E1-E6).

Task: <FIGURE> (e.g. the E1 figure: average wait vs load).

Rules:
- Read only the summary CSV files (data/sample_summaries/ or results/summaries/). Never run experiments, call the C program, or compute statistics.
- Use only pandas and matplotlib. Short functions, clear names, a comment on every block. No clever one-liners, no classes.
- One figure per function. Title, labelled axes with units, legend, and error bars or shaded 95% bands from the ci_low / ci_high columns.
- Save PNG and PDF into docs/report/figures/ using the shared style.
- Explain each step before writing it, in simple language. After the figure, explain how to read it and what it shows.
```

**From PRD §5 Summary CSV formats (policy values):**

- UTF-8, comma-separated, one header row, no index column, `.` as the decimal point, no thousands separators. A missing value is an empty field.
- Long format: one row per (experiment, setting, policy), plus one extra key where stated (E3 adds the priority level through `x_value`).
- Key columns, always first and in this order: `experiment` (`E1` … `E6`), `setting` (text label of the varied parameter), `x_value` (the number to put on the x-axis), `policy` (`fcfs`, `priority`, `sjf`, `aging`, `reserve`, `knapsack`), `n_seeds` (number of seeds or instances averaged; the same for every metric in the row).
- For every metric `<m>` three columns follow: `<m>_mean`, `<m>_ci_low`, `<m>_ci_high`.
- **Confidence interval.** Two-sided 95% Student-t interval of the mean across seeds: mean ± t · s / √n, with s the sample standard deviation (n − 1 in the denominator). The t value is a hard-coded constant: t(0.975, df = 29) = 2.045 for n = 30 seeds; t(0.975, df = 49) = 2.010 for the E6 groups of 50 instances. Source and rounding are recorded in `DECISIONS.md`. Any other n is an error in `summarize.py`.
- Time metrics are in ticks; utilisations are fractions from 0 to 1; ratios have no unit.

## 3. Scope

**In scope:**

- `apply_style()` setting font sizes and grid
- A fixed dictionary policy → (colour, line style, marker) for `fcfs`, `priority`, `sjf`, `aging`, `reserve`, `knapsack`
- `save_figure(fig, name, out_dir)` writing `<name>.png` and `<name>.pdf`
- Redrawing the A-01 figure with the style

**Out of scope:**

- Error bars and other figures (A-03)
- Captions (A-06)

## 5. Specification

```python
POLICY_LOOK = {"fcfs": (...), "priority": (...), "sjf": (...), "aging": (...), "reserve": (...), "knapsack": (...)}  # colour, linestyle, marker
def apply_style() -> None: ...
def save_figure(fig, name: str, out_dir: str) -> list[str]: ...  # returns the two paths
```
Colours must stay distinguishable in greyscale: each policy also has its own line style and marker, so colour is never the only difference. Axis labels always include units (ticks, jobs per tick, %, or "ratio").

## 6. Step-by-step tasks

1. Explain to Ahaana why greyscale matters (printed reports)
2. Write `POLICY_LOOK`
3. Write `apply_style`
4. Write `save_figure`
5. Redraw E1 and print it in greyscale to check

## 8. Acceptance criteria (Done when)

- [ ] Every policy has a fixed colour + line style + marker, readable when printed in greyscale
- [ ] PNG and PDF written for the E1 sample figure
- [ ] Every block commented; Ahaana can explain why each style choice helps the reader
- [ ] Only pandas and matplotlib

## 9. How to verify

```sh
python tools/plot_figures.py && ls docs/report/figures/
```
A pass: `e1_avg_wait.png` and `e1_avg_wait.pdf` exist and look identical.

## 10. Viva notes

**How to read it:** each scheduler keeps the same look in every figure, so the reader learns the legend once.
**Examiner question:** "Why markers and dashes as well as colours?" — So the figure still works printed in black and white, and for colour-blind readers.

## 11. Pitfalls

- Changing global matplotlib state in many places
- Saving PDF with a different size than PNG
- Using red/green as the only distinction
